sentences.text:
Accused JUDGMENT:
1.
The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused has violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules.
The accused is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s. Paramjeet Machhiwala, from where the food article, that is, 'Refined Groundnut Oil' was lifted for sampling.

2. As per the complaint, on 13.01.2003, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI)
V.P.S.Chaudhary and FI R.K.Bhaskar under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. M.A.Ashraf reached along with their staff at M/s. Paramjeet Machhiwala at WZ-1, Shop No. 9,
Basai Darapur, New Delhi, where the accused was found conducting the business of various food articles which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption.

The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Refined Groundnut Oil from the vendor (ready for use), lying in an open container, bearing no label declaration, to which he agreed.
The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.

Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot,
including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc.
The price of sample was offered to the vendor but he did not accept the same.

Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Jeevan Singh on 6 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150222830/
1 Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.

sentences.text:
Vide report dated 05.02.2003, the PA found the sample to be non-conforming to the standards of Groundnut Oil because B.R. and Iodine values exceeded the prescribed maximum limits and B.T.T.
was less than prescribed minimum limit.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by the FI.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.
The complaint was then filed in the court on 21.07.2003 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act, as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 21.07.2003.
The accused appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising his right to get the second counterpart of the sample analysed from the Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL.

The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 13.10.2003, opining the sample to be not conform to the standards of Groundnut oil on the ground that B.R. and Iodine values exceeded the prescribed maximum limits and B.T.T. was less than prescribed minimum limit.
4. On the basis of CFL report, the matter was listed for pre-charge evidence wherein the complainant examined PW-1 FI V.P.S.Chaudhary as the only witness.

Based on his deposition,
charge was framed against the accused on 08.04.2009 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1) PFA Act, being violation of Section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

The witness examined in pre-charge stage was recalled for further cross-examination in post charge stage and additionally, the complainant examined PW-2 FI R.K.Bhaskar and PW-3 Sh. M.A.Ashraf in post charge stage.
5. PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 13.01.2003 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity,
expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 375 gms of Refined Groundnut Oil (ready for use) after proper mixing with the help of clean and dry karachi by rotating it in all possible directions several times, dividing it in three parts and putting in clean and dry bottles, then separately packing, fastening, sealing and marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex.
PW- 1/A, Notice as per Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B and Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C.

On the next working day,
one counterpart of sample along with Memo as per Form-VII were sent to PA vide PA receipt Ex.
PW-1/D for analysis and remaining two counterparts with copy of Memos were deposited with LHA/SDM vide receipt Ex. PW-1/E.
PA report Ex. PW-1/F was received and upon direction of SDM/LHA, further investigation was carried out by PW-1.
Letter Ex. PW-1/G was sent to the accused and accused submitted photocopy of the MCD registration.
Letter Ex. PW-1/H was sent to the STO.

Thereafter, sanction Ex. PW-1/J was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex.
PW-1/K was filed in the court.
Intimation Letter Ex. PW-1/L was sent to the accused along with copy of PA report through post.

The witnesses were duly cross-examined by the defence wherein they Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Jeevan Singh on 6 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150222830/
2 denied that the sample was not taken properly or that different samples were put in different bottles or that the accused had been falsely implicated.

sentences.text: 6. Statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 03.07.2013 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
He claimed that the oil was not for sale as such and that the sampling method was not proper.
He claimed that no adulteration was made by him.
He however did not lead any evidence in defence.

7. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused has not been able to rebut the findings in the CFL report dated 13.10.2003 which as per section 13(3) and (5) of PFA Act is final and conclusive.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.

8. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various contradictions and missing links in the testimony of witnesses.
It is pointed out that the PA and CFL reports would show that the samples sent to them were not of the same food article and were not in the same container.
It is argued that different samples had been lifted by the FI which were sent to different analysts, which would go to the root of the matter, the benefit of which should be given to the accused.
9. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.

10. For section 2(ia)(a) PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.

Section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.
11. As per section 13(3) of the PFA Act, the certificate issued by the Director of CFL shall supersede the report of the PA.
As per proviso to section 13(5) of the Act, such certificate shall be final and conclusive evidence for the facts stated therein.

Thus, as far as the findings of the CFL are concerned, the same are final and conclusive and no evidence can be given to disprove the same.
12.

In Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738], it has been authoritatively laid down that the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of CFL is three fold: (a)
it annuls or replaces the report of the PA, (b) it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and (c) it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned.

entities.text: Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 13. Since the report of CFL is final and conclusive and the same supersedes the report of PA, only this report has to be considered and the report of PA has to be ignored.

However, the defence Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Jeevan Singh on 6 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150222830/
3 strongly relies upon the judgement titled as Kanshi Nath v. State [2005(2) FAC 219], informing that the said ruling has been constantly followed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in State v. sentences.text: It is submitted that comparison of the two reports would show that there are substantive variations which would show that the sample was not representative.

14. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Kashi Nath's case (supra), was dealing with a situation where there were certain variations in the reports of PA and CFL while analysing a sample of 'dhania powder'.

Hon'ble Court considered the ratio in MCD v. Bishan Sarup [ILR 1970 (1) Delhi 518] and held that it would still be open for the accused to establish that the sample tested was not a representative one, and if the variation in the two reports is substantial enough, then the PA report can certainly be looked into to establish this variation.

15. Therefore, it can be safely said that though the CFL report is final and conclusive as to the results therein, yet it can still be looked into to ascertain if the samples were representative or not.
If the accused is able to show that the samples were not representative, he would get benefit on that count.

16. In the present case, it has been admitted by PW-1 that 'groundnut oil' and 'refined groundnut oil'
are two separate food articles, having different characteristics and having different standards under the PFA Act.
During his cross-
examination
, he stated that both the food articles can be distinguished even with naked eyes as the refined groundnut oil is colourless and the colour of groundnut oil is pale yellow.
He denied that he had lifted a sample of pale yellow coloured oil in a sealed bottle of manufacturer, alongwith a sample from another container.
17. As per the complainant and as can be seen from the documents prepared at the spot, the sample was that of a 'refined groundnut oil'.
The vendor receipt Ex. PW-1/A, Form VI Ex. PW-1/B and the LHA Receipt PW-1/E all mentioned the food article to be refined groundnut oil.
Even the PA report Ex. PW-1/F
shows that the sample received by it was that of 'refined groundnut oil'.
18. However, the CFL report dated 13.10.2003 would show substantive differences as to the identity of the food article sought to be analysed.
The CFL found the sample to be that of 'groundnut oil' (as against 'refined groundnut oil' as was lifted).

Further, the sample was described to be received in "manufacturer's sealed glass bottle" (as against the prosecution version that the sample was in loose condition which was packed in the sample glass bottle).

Not only this, the CFL found the physical appearance of the sample to be 'pale yellow liquid' (as against the colourless liquid of 'refined groundnut oil' that was lifted).
19.
It is thus seen that there is apparent variation in the two samples that were sent to different analysts.

Even the CFL was not sure if the sample sent to it was that of groundnut oil or refined Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Jeevan Singh on 6 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150222830/
4 groundnut oil, as it mentioned the sample to be falling under Item No. A.17.03 as well as A.17.15 of Appendix-B of PFA Rules.

sentences.text:
Of course the CFL certificate supersedes the PA Report as to its finding,
yet such a rule would apply only when both the samples are established to be of the same product,
same lot / batch and representative of each other.
If two samples belonged to different food articles or the food article is not homogenised properly to make it representative, then the benefit would go to the accused.

20. The version of PW-1 that the sample was not of pale yellow colour and that it was not in manufacturer's sealed glass bottle, stood negated by the observation of the Director CFL which found the sample to be that of groundnut oil of pale yellow colour and sent in manufacturer's sealed glass bottle.
If the stand of the prosecution was to be revealed the sample with the CFL should have been of a colourless liquid and in sample glass bottle and should be that of refined groundnut oil.
Such observation of CFL cannot be termed as clerical mistake or a typographical error.
It was the duty of the prosecution to have ruled out all such discrepancies appearing in its case.
But despite such defence taken by the accused even during the cross-examination of PW-1 no attempt was made by it to summon the necessary record from the CFL and to clarify the position.
A doubt has certainly been created as to the genuineness of the samples seized at the spot.
The possibility that the two samples were not of the same product or of same lot and therefore not representative, cannot be ruled out.
21. In a criminal trial, the burden is upon the complainant / prosecution to establish its case beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt.
To bring home the guilt of an accused, it has to stands on its own legs and lead positive evidence.
Mere suspicion, howsoever strong it might be, cannot take place of proof required to establish guilt of an accused.
This burden has to be discharged by the prosecution and it cannot be shifted upon the accused.
22. The present case is based only on the testimony of food officials.
There is no independent public person joined by the officials in the sample proceedings as provided by section 10(7) of PFA Act.

The court is well aware of the reluctance of public persons to join such legal proceedings that involves lengthy procedural formalities and strict future commitments and that non joining of such witnesses would not negate the testimony of official witnesses, but in such a case, the testimony of such witnesses has to be otherwise truthful, corroborative and credit worthy.
Such evidence should be free from fatal inconsistencies and contradictions.

23. But in the present case, the evidence of PW-1 has been contradicted by the document of the prosecution itself in the form of CFL report, which cannot be said to be minor in nature which could be ignored easily.
24. With such contradictory material, it would not be safe to rely upon it to establish guilt of the accused.
Possibility of improper or invalid sampling method and procedure cannot be ruled out.

25. In view of the above discussed circumstances, this court is of the view that the complainant in this case has not been able to establish beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt that the accused had sold or stored for sale any adulterated food article.

The accused is entitled to be given benefit of Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Jeevan Singh on 6 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150222830/
5 doubt.
26.

sentences.text: Having said so, the accused is acquitted of the charges.

However, his bail bond shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A, CrPC.
27.
